title: Metropolis 3.0 to Build a Profitable Business Through Capacity, Science and Technology Investments
summary: Metropolis Healthcare is banking on a richer test mix, higher network utilisation and operational efficiencies to drive growth and margin expansion, following a 10 per cent rise in patient volumes and 11 per cent growth in test volumes without a price...
thbAction: Map the news to THB's provider CRM for referral growth, patient lifecycle engagement, and multi-facility relationship management across hospital and provider networks.
contentHtml:
New Delhi : Surendran Chemmenkotil, Managing Director, Metropolis Healthcare Ltd spoke exclusively to ETHealthworld about Metropolis 3.0 strategy is shifting from network expansion to deeper utilisation, specialty diagnostics and technology-led growth. He discusses the drivers of margin expansion, rising demand for preventive and advanced testing, the economics of smaller-town markets, and the company's focus on building a more scalable, profitable business through investments in capacity, science and technology.

Metropolis reported 15.8 per cent revenue growth to Rs 496.8 crore in Q2 FY27, while EBITDA grew 23.9 per cent to Rs 134.9 crore and PAT increased 42.7 per cent to Rs 75.5 crore. EBITDA margins also expanded 180 basis points to 27.2 per cent. What were the key drivers behind this improvement in profitability? How much came from operating leverage, higher test volumes, improved test mix and operational efficiencies?

Advt

This has been a strong quarter, and the improvement in profitability has come from the core of our business. Patient volumes grew 10 per cent and test volumes 11 per cent, while a richer test mix lifted realisations. As a large part of our cost base is fixed, this volume growth translated into healthy operating leverage, and our EBITDA margin expanded 180 basis points to 27.2 per cent, ahead of our guidance of 125 to 175 basis points. We have delivered this without any price increase so far this year, with growth driven purely by volumes and test mix.

Productivity has been the other big contributor. Our manpower base has remained broadly stable even as test volumes grew, and our laboratories are processing more samples a day on the same fixed costs. Disciplined cost management and the steady replacement of manual processes with technology have added to these gains. We do not attribute the improvement to any single factor, because these levers work together: higher volumes improve network utilisation, a better mix lifts realisations, and productivity allows us to protect margins as we scale.

Patient volumes grew 10 per cent and test volumes 11 per cent, while revenue per patient increased 6 per cent to Rs 1,221 and revenue per test rose 5 per cent to Rs 572, despite no price increase. What is driving the improvement in realisations? How much is attributable to premiumisation, a richer test mix and increased adoption of specialised tests?

The improvement in realisations is being driven by our test mix, not by pricing. Two parts of our portfolio, TruHealth and Specialty, are growing faster than the overall business, and both carry a higher value per visit. TruHealth, our preventive health segment, now contributes around 17 per cent of revenue, with an average ticket size of approximately Rs 2,400 to Rs 2,500, well above that of a routine test. Specialty contributes around 40 per cent of revenue, and we added 43 specialty and super-specialty tests in the first half alone.

Advt

As more people opt for comprehensive health packages and clinicians increasingly prescribe advanced tests in oncology and genomics, the value of each patient visit rises. The growth in revenue per patient and revenue per test is a direct reflection of this shift in how diagnostics is being used in India.You had earlier indicated that Metropolis would prioritise improving utilisation over expanding into more cities, with a target of increasing the collection centre-to-lab ratio from 21–22 to 30. With the network now spanning approximately 750 towns and 5,119 service points, how much progress has been made towards this target? What is the current utilisation level of the laboratory network?

Advt

Improving the utilisation of our laboratory network remains a key priority, and we are making steady progress. Over the last few years, we built laboratory capacity across our markets, and our focus has now shifted to strengthening the collection network that feeds these laboratories. The number of collection centres per laboratory has increased from approximately 21 in FY25 to around 24 today, and we aim to take this to 30 and then towards 35 over the next two years.During the quarter, we added 116 collection centres, taking our net additions over the last 24 months to nearly 700. We will accelerate this in the second half, both to cover the areas around the laboratories we set up in FY25 and FY26 and to go deeper in markets where we are already strong. These newer laboratories are gaining good traction, and every collection point we add around them increases throughput without adding to our fixed costs.

With revenue growing faster than patient volumes, how much additional business can the existing laboratory infrastructure absorb before fresh investments in capacity become necessary? Where are the current capacity constraints?We have meaningful headroom in our existing infrastructure. Between FY21 and FY25, we expanded laboratory capacity by close to 50 per cent and invested significantly in technology, so our network can absorb considerably more volume before fresh capacity is needed. The real constraint today is reach rather than laboratory capacity, which is why we are directing our investments towards bringing more samples into the laboratories we already have.In the near term, our spending will be focused on collection centres, B2B partnerships, mini-hubs, technology and specialised capabilities. Mini-hubs are larger centres that bring pathology, basic radiology and doctor consultations together under one roof, closer to where patients live and work. We will continue to add laboratory capacity selectively, where a specific market or a new specialty capability requires it, but we will not build infrastructure ahead of demand.Is the B2C business continuing to deliver better margins? How do you see the revenue mix evolving over the next two to three years? As your B2C revenue grew 17 per cent to Rs 289 crore, while B2B revenue increased 15 per cent to Rs 208 crore.Our B2C business delivered healthy growth this quarter, supported by new-patient acquisition as well as a stronger performance from our established centres. Existing centres recorded same-store growth of approximately 10 per cent, while newer centres continued to ramp up, so we are getting more out of our existing network as well as from new openings. A direct relationship with patients also allows us to serve them across diagnostics and preventive health over a longer period.B2C currently contributes around 58 per cent of our revenue, but we do not manage the business towards a predetermined mix. B2B is equally important to us, because it takes our specialty portfolio to hospitals, laboratories and clinicians and adds scale to our laboratory operations. Our aim is for both channels to grow sustainably and strengthen the overall quality of our business.You had earlier spoken about improving the quality of B2B business and moving away from low-quality institutional accounts. Is the current B2B growth translating into better profitability, or does the segment continue to face pricing pressure?We have been very deliberate about the kind of B2B business we want to build. We consciously exited institutional contracts that were driven purely by price, and we are now adding good-quality institutional and partner business where our science, test menu, quality and service create real value. This shift is now reflected in our numbers.During the quarter, B2B patient volumes grew 7 per cent while test volumes grew 11 per cent, which means our partners are sending us more tests per patient, including specialised tests. That is a clear sign that partners value our specialty capabilities.Our partner network has now crossed around 9,000, and our partner portal makes it simpler for partners to work with us, with better visibility, quicker turnaround and seamless access to our full test menu. With hospitals, we focus on areas where our specialised testing complements their clinical needs. Our objective is to build durable partnerships, not simply to add volumes.As you mentioned, TruHealth and Specialty are growing faster than the overall business. What is driving demand in these two segments? Are preventive health check-ups and specialty testing becoming meaningful contributors to the company's overall growth and margins?Both TruHealth and Specialty grew around 20 per cent this quarter and are firmly established as our strategic growth engines. In preventive health, people are far more health-conscious today and are choosing regular check-ups and early screening instead of visiting a laboratory only when they fall ill. Packages that include radiology are gaining traction, supported by add-ons such as doctor consultations, vitals checks and ECG. We are now extending these services beyond our own centres to our mature franchise network, so that patients can complete all their recommended tests and consultations with us, in one place, under one trusted brand.In Specialty, growth is coming from wider adoption of advanced tests, deeper engagement with clinicians and a steadily expanding test menu. Specialty also creates a halo effect for our routine business, because a patient who comes to us for a specialised test naturally prefers to complete the rest of their tests with us. We expect both segments to contribute a growing share of our revenue in the years ahead.Specialty diagnostics growth is being supported by genomics and cancer testing. With the introduction of a 1,000-gene oncology panel and a blood-based Alzheimer's test, what is the commercial opportunity for high-end diagnostics in India? How do you address affordability and access beyond metro markets?We see a significant long-term opportunity in high-end diagnostics. In areas such as oncology, reproductive health and rare and inherited disorders, testing is moving beyond identifying a disease to understanding its molecular and genetic basis, which directly guides treatment decisions. Success in this space depends far more on scientific depth than on equipment, spanning molecular pathology, genetics, genetic counselling and bioinformatics, along with the confidence of clinicians. We have built these capabilities through our genomics laboratories in Gurgaon and Mumbai, and our genomics portfolio has roughly doubled in a year.Our 1,000-gene oncology panel and blood-based Alzheimer’s test are examples of how we are bringing earlier answers to complex clinical questions. On affordability, scale will be the deciding factor. As volumes grow and technology evolves, the cost of advanced testing will come down, and our centralised testing model allows us to offer these tests across the country without duplicating expensive infrastructure. In parallel, we are building awareness among specialists through a series of genomics symposiums across India.Tier III cities recorded approximately 20 per cent revenue growth, ahead of the company's overall growth of 15.8 per cent. What is driving this demand? Is the shift towards organised diagnostics accelerating in smaller towns, and what are the economics of operating in these markets?The shift towards organised diagnostics is clearly gathering pace beyond the metros. Health awareness is rising, local healthcare infrastructure is improving, and patients and doctors in smaller towns are placing a much higher value on accuracy and reliability. Our Tier III and rural centres led our growth this quarter and now contribute around 26 per cent of our domestic revenue, with growth broad-based across all four regions.The economics of these markets are attractive because our model is asset-light. Collection centres, a significant proportion of which operate as franchises, extend our reach while the testing is done in laboratories we already operate. Franchise centres typically break even within three to four months, and most within six, while company-owned centres generally take 12 to 18 months to reach healthy margins. This gives us a capital-efficient route to deepen our presence in smaller towns, where improving access to healthcare is creating a large and growing base of new patients.Specialty diagnostics remain concentrated in larger cities. What needs to change for advanced testing to become more accessible in tier II and tier III markets? Will this require investments in local infrastructure, technology or partnerships with hospitals and clinicians?Advanced testing can become far more accessible in Tier II and Tier III markets without a specialised laboratory in every city. What it needs is a point of care close to the patient, with complex testing carried out at centres that have the right expertise and technology. We are focusing on three elements to make this work: a strong collection and logistics network; technology that connects the patient, laboratory and clinician; and deeper engagement with doctors in these markets. We are also planning around 100 mini-hubs over the next three years to bring basic radiology, consultations and faster reporting within easy reach of patients.Regulatory and technological developments are supporting this. The National Medical Commission has recently clarified that a registered medical practitioner can remotely review and authenticate reports using a recognised digital signature. This means a complex haematology or oncology case from a smaller town can be reviewed by a sub-specialist in our reference laboratory. It also allows us to set up smaller laboratories faster, supported by a central pool of pathologists. Technology is improving turnaround times as well; AI-assisted karyotyping, for instance, has reduced reporting time from approximately 15 days to around seven days. As we expand our reach, every report will continue to be reviewed by a qualified pathologist, because quality is non-negotiable for us.Core Diagnostics has moved from break-even levels at the time of acquisition to near double-digit EBITDA margins, according to your latest commentary. With the acquisition strengthening Metropolis' oncology and specialty diagnostics portfolio, how much has it contributed to revenue growth and profitability? What remains to be done to bring its margins closer to Metropolis' overall levels?Core Diagnostics is a strong example of how we create value through acquisitions. It was operating at break-even when we acquired it a year ago and is now delivering near double-digit EBITDA margins. Its larger value, however, lies in what it brings to our platform. We are using our distribution network to cross-sell Core’s oncology and genomics tests across our customer and partner base. This is driving strong traction in Specialty and has also accelerated the growth of our own genomics business.During the first year, our focus was on integration, including a planned restructuring of the team, and that work is now complete. With this in place, our attention shifts to accelerating revenue, and we expect Core to deliver stronger growth with improving margins over the rest of the year.With the existing network now spanning approximately 750 towns, what kind of acquisitions are you looking at going forward? Are you prioritising regional diagnostic chains, specialty laboratories or technology-led capabilities? How are valuations influencing acquisition decisions?We will remain selective. For us, an acquisition must either strengthen our position in an important market or add capabilities that create long-term value, and scale by itself is not a reason to buy. We prefer established businesses with a strong local reputation and high standards of ethics and transparency, which can benefit from our specialty test menu, technology, procurement, quality systems and logistics. North India remains a priority, and we will keep evaluating opportunities across pathology and relevant ancillary services there.The four acquisitions we completed over the past year are performing well and integrating smoothly. Dr Ahujas’ Pathology and Imaging Centre in Dehradun and Scientific Pathology in Agra are growing in line with the company average while delivering margins above our overall margins, and together with Core, they have raised North India’s share to around 17 per cent of our domestic revenue.We are equally disciplined on valuations. Some good-quality businesses have recently been acquired at very high valuations, but in diagnostics, margins usually dip during integration before they recover, so paying a steep price makes it very difficult to earn a reasonable return. When we acquire at the right price and build value ourselves through our brand, test menu, logistics and procurement, the returns are far healthier. We will therefore not pay a premium simply to add revenue or geographical presence.Revenue per patient increased 6 per cent and revenue per test rose 5 per cent, despite no price increase benefit. How much of this improvement is attributable to premiumisation and a richer test mix? With operating costs continuing to be a factor for diagnostic providers, how will Metropolis sustain margin expansion without compromising affordability for patients?The improvement in our realisations this year has come entirely from the shift in our test mix, without any contribution from pricing, so we have not had to trade affordability for margin. Going forward, sustaining our margins will depend largely on efficiency, and we have several levers in place.Our transition to a common laboratory platform, which standardises the test menu, equipment, reagents and turnaround times across our network while consolidating vendors, will be completed in the third quarter and will support gross margins. We are replacing manual processes with technology across sample logistics, reporting and back-office functions, and greater network density will further improve the efficiency of each laboratory. Together, these measures allow us to protect margins through mix, productivity and scale, so that patients continue to receive high-quality diagnostics at fair prices.Metropolis 3.0 places emphasis on science, genomics, technology and strategic acquisitions rather than simply expanding its geographical footprint. What will be the measurable business priorities under this strategy over the next two to three years? What should investors and the industry expect to see change in the company's business model?Metropolis 3.0 is about converting our investments in capacity, science and technology into a more scalable and profitable business. The strategy rests on four pillars: leading with technology, differentiating ourselves scientifically, delivering consistent and profitable growth, and strengthening our brand promise of trust.Our priorities over the next two to three years are clear and measurable. We will take network density towards 35 collection centres for every laboratory, establish around 100 mini-hubs, add B2B partners faster with a sharper focus on specialty, and continue to expand beyond the metros. We also expect Specialty and Preventive Health to account for a larger share of our portfolio, supported by new tests in genomics and oncology.Technology will underpin each of these priorities. Over the coming months, we are rolling out a new CRM platform, a dynamic pricing engine and a sales app for our field teams, while strengthening integration with hospital partners so they can connect seamlessly with our systems. AI is being scaled across customer engagement, laboratory operations and quality, and our systems are being aligned with the Digital Personal Data Protection framework. For investors and the industry, the change will be visible in higher productivity, a more premium portfolio and growth that relies less on adding new infrastructure.Patient volumes increased 10 per cent, while test volumes grew 11 per cent. Does this indicate that existing patients are opting for more tests, or is the growth primarily coming from new patient acquisition? What does this tell you about changing diagnostic utilisation patterns in India?Both are contributing. New patients are entering the organised diagnostics ecosystem, while existing patients and partners are using a wider range of tests. In B2C, new-patient acquisition remains strong, supported by targeted customer engagement, focused micro-market campaigns, growing brand pull and wider use of our digital platforms. In B2B, partners are sending us more of their specialised testing.More broadly, the way India uses diagnostics is changing. This year’s monsoon was one of the weakest in over two decades, and the usual seasonal rise in infections such as dengue and malaria was uneven across regions. Even so, our revenue grew around 16 per cent, which shows that our growth does not depend only on seasonal demand. It is also driven by the underlying strength of our portfolio across chronic disease management, preventive health and specialty testing. Diagnostics today plays a role across prevention, diagnosis and treatment, and this creates a structural opportunity for quality-focused, organised players like Metropolis.
